meta.subtitle: Global alternative asset manager with over $1 trillion of AUM; revenue growth is accelerating, but the dividend runs ahead of free cash flow

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. (BAM) a BUY with a $50 to $58 target range. BAM, which describes itself as a leading global alternative asset manager, invests client capital across infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate, and credit, and earns asset management income for doing so. FY25 revenue rose {+ +21.0% +} to $4.8B after a small dip in FY24, and Q2'26 revenue grew {+ +60.8% +} year over year to $1.8B. FY25 net income reached $2.4B and the trailing net margin is 53.4%. The shares trade at $46.01, near the bottom of a $42.20 to $62.57 52-week range, at 26.6x trailing earnings and about 21.2x consensus FY27E EPS. The Street reads Buy on consensus with a $57.52 target, but its 18 analysts split 9 Buy, 8 Hold and 1 Sell. Our probability-weighted expected upside is +11.9% against a bear-case downside of {- -20.5% -}, a reward/risk of 0.58x. That clears the BUY line by a narrow margin, and the valuation section explains what decides it. Dividends have exceeded free cash flow in each of the last three years, and the pack does not show how much of the recent revenue jump is organic; both keep conviction moderate.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. describes itself as a leading global alternative asset manager, headquartered in New York, with over $1 trillion of Assets Under Management across infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate, and credit. It offers alternative investment products to over 2,500 institutional clients, alongside a private-wealth client base that the company says continues to grow, with approximately 69,000 clients. It earns asset management income for doing so. The company runs 59 unique active strategies and draws on over 5,800 investment and asset management professionals and employees across 32 global offices, with a dedicated team of approximately 150 people focused on the private wealth channel. Its products fall into long-term private funds, permanent capital vehicles and perpetual strategies, and liquid strategies, invested across five principal strategies. The Class A Shares are co-listed on the NYSE and the TSX under the symbol BAM. Per the 10-Q's MD&A, the company evaluates the performance of its product offerings and investment strategies with non-GAAP measures, including Fee-Bearing Capital, Fee Revenues, Fee-Related Earnings and Distributable Earnings.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body: The case rests on a top line that is accelerating faster than the consensus estimates assume, at a price that asks little of the earnings path consensus already expects. The Base case needs only that those estimates arrive and that the market hold its current-year multiple a year out; it does not need a re-rating. What tempers the case is the quality of the growth and of the payout. Earnings have lagged revenue, the dividend leans on sources beyond free cash flow, and the pack cannot separate organic growth from consolidation effects. The financials, growth and valuation sections carry the figures. On balance the expected return clears the BUY line, though narrowly.

catalysts: Delivery of consensus FY26E and FY27E EPS would carry the Base case, which needs no re-rating.
Further quarters of revenue growth well ahead of the full-year estimate would support the consensus earnings path.
Growth in Fee-Bearing Capital across the five platforms, including the AI infrastructure and private-wealth products, would lift fee income.
A move back toward the Street's consensus target would recover part of the slide from the 52-week high.
risks: The dividend has exceeded free cash flow in each of the last three fiscal years, and total equity has edged lower.
The pack does not separate organic growth from consolidation effects, so the latest quarter may overstate the underlying pace.
Part of BAM's FY25 results sat outside management's internal-control evaluation, per the 10-K.
The shares have de-rated toward their 52-week low with no source in the pack explaining why, and the Street is split almost evenly between Buy and Hold.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue was $4.1B in FY23 and dipped {- -2.0% -} to $4.0B in FY24, then rose {+ +21.0% +} to $4.8B in FY25. Net income was $2.1B in both FY23 and FY24 and rose to $2.4B in FY25. Diluted EPS climbed from $1.16 to $1.34 to $1.52 over the same span. As an asset manager, BAM reports no gross-margin, operating-income or EBITDA line, so margin analysis runs through net income. The trailing net margin is 53.4%, which still reflects an asset-light fee model. In Q2'26, the quarter ended June 30, 2026, revenue was $1.8B, up {+ +60.8% +} year over year; with no operating-income line, the quarter's operating margin is not meaningful. Of the company's own non-GAAP measures, the pack gives values only for Fee-Bearing Capital. The top line is the stronger half of the story: net income grew more slowly than revenue in FY25, so the revenue acceleration has not yet shown up as wider margins.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet the pack shows is light on detail. Cash and short-term investments rose from $0.0B in FY23 to $0.4B in FY24 and $1.6B in FY25. Total equity edged down over the same years, from $9.3B in FY23 to $9.1B in FY24 and $8.9B in FY25. The pack does not disclose total debt, net debt or a current ratio, and net debt/EBITDA and interest coverage are blank, so leverage and liquidity coverage cannot be assessed from it. We read the balance sheet as adequate on cash but unmeasurable on leverage. The slow decline in equity while cash builds is consistent with a payout that has outrun earnings, which the cash-flow discussion takes up.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow rose each year, from $1.4B in FY23. Capital expenditure is negligible, so free cash flow matched operating cash flow in each year, and the FCF margin widened from 35.0% in FY23 to 40.3% in FY24 and 43.4% in FY25. The trailing FCF yield is 3.2%. The pressure point is the payout. Dividends paid rose to $2.5B in FY24 and $2.8B in FY25, and they exceeded free cash flow in each of the three years; the FY25 payment also exceeded FY25 net income. Cash still rose over the period, which implies the gap was filled outside these lines; the pack does not detail financing flows. A payout that runs ahead of free cash flow is sustainable only while other sources fill the gap. We therefore treat coverage of the distribution as the main cash-flow question, even as free cash flow itself improves.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $46.01, near the 52-week low of $42.20 and well below the high of $62.57, BAM trades at 26.6x trailing earnings, 12.8x sales and about 21.2x consensus FY27E EPS. The vendor labels its 25.1x forward multiple next-twelve-month, but it matches the price over consensus FY26E EPS, so we read it as a current-year multiple. The snapshot also shows EV/EBITDA of 20.4x, although the statements carry no EBITDA line, so we do not rely on it. The peer column is empty, with peers pending a peer data source, so we anchor the scenarios to the company's own consensus EPS path rather than to a comparable set. The 4.35% dividend yield sits above the 3.2% FCF yield, the coverage gap covered under financials. The Street's consensus target is $57.52 and its median $55.50, with targets ranging from $44.00 to $70.00.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Fee-Bearing Capital grows across the five platforms and consensus FY27E EPS of $2.17 arrives. The market pays 28x for it, a re-rating of about three turns above today's current-year multiple; we allow it because the shares traded above the resulting price at their 52-week high. That gives $60.76.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus FY27E EPS arrives and, a year out, the shares hold 25x, about today's current-year multiple carried forward. Fee income keeps pace with the estimates, but the market does not re-rate the stock while the dividend runs ahead of earnings. That gives $54.25, below the consensus target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Higher-for-longer rates slow fundraising, the latest quarter's revenue jump does not carry into FY27, and EPS stalls near the FY26E consensus of $1.83. The market pays 20x, about five turns below today's current-year multiple, as it stops paying for growth and doubts the dividend's coverage. That gives $36.60, below the 52-week low and the lowest Street target.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 50% and the Bull and Bear at 25% each. The weighted fair value is about $51, an expected upside of +11.9% against a bear-case downside of {- -20.5% -}, for a reward/risk of 0.58x. The rule derives BUY, and we publish BUY. The call is close, and the Base multiple decides it. On one basis, the Base holds today's current-year multiple a year out, which equals today's price plus one year of consensus EPS growth; a Base one turn lower would derive HOLD. The case for holding the multiple is that the growth behind it is still visible a year out: the latest quarter's revenue growth runs well ahead of the FY26E estimate, and consensus EPS keeps rising into FY27E. The case against is that the shares have already de-rated from the 52-week high toward the low with no source in the pack explaining the move, and that the dividend runs ahead of earnings. We judge the evidence behind the estimates the stronger of the two, so we keep the multiple, and we treat the BUY as fragile. The Bull is a true re-rating, not a modest premium, and we weight it no higher than the Bear for that reason. The Bear weight rests on the Bear story itself. A de-rating is already under way and dividend coverage is thin. Against that, a stall in EPS would have to follow a quarter of {+ +60.8% +} revenue growth, which is why we do not weight it higher. Our $50 to $58 target range brackets the Base case.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: BAM reports a single reportable segment, and the vendor breaks out no product or geographic revenue mix. The segment table carries the FY25 consolidated total at $3.9B, which disagrees with the $4.8B of FY25 revenue in the income statement; we use the income-statement figure throughout. Underneath the single segment, the company runs five investment platforms, shown here by AUM and Fee-Bearing Capital (FBC) as of June 30, 2026. Credit leads by scale at $416B of AUM and $326B of FBC. Real estate carries $280B of AUM and $104B of FBC. Infrastructure holds $262B of AUM and $114B of FBC and includes a dedicated AI infrastructure fund. Private equity holds $166B of AUM and $54B of FBC. Energy holds $144B of AUM and $74B of FBC across transition and renewable strategies. Two listed vehicles anchor the permanent-capital base: an infrastructure platform with a $29.3B market capitalization and a renewable platform with a market capitalization of over $24.4B, both as of June 30, 2026.

moatFactors.name: Scale in alternatives
moatFactors.body: Over $1 trillion of AUM spans five platforms. The company says its operating expertise, global reach and access to large-scale flexible capital let it make sizable investments that it believes few others can, which supports fundraising for large funds.

moatFactors.name: Permanent and perpetual capital
moatFactors.body: Products include permanent capital vehicles and perpetual strategies alongside long-term private funds, so part of Fee-Bearing Capital is long-dated and less exposed to redemption, which steadies fee income across cycles.

moatFactors.name: Diversified fee base
moatFactors.body: Fee-Bearing Capital is spread across all five platforms, so a weak year in one asset class is cushioned by the others. Credit holds far more Fee-Bearing Capital than any other platform, which concentrates exposure more than the five-way split suggests.

moatFactors.name: Client and distribution reach
moatFactors.body: The client base spans institutional investors and a private-wealth channel served by a dedicated team. Breadth of channel keeps fundraising diversified across client types, which supports fee stability when any single pool of capital pulls back.

businessMoat.durability: The platforms above are presented by AUM and Fee-Bearing Capital, not as a revenue split, because the company reports one consolidated segment. The durability of the fee base rests on long-dated and perpetual capital and on a diversified set of active strategies, which should smooth fundraising cycles; the rising FCF margin described under financials is consistent with that. The main threat is external: the business is sensitive to market and interest-rate conditions, as set out under systemic risk. On balance the moat is real but not impregnable, which is why we rate it narrow rather than wide.

points: Consensus expects FY26E revenue of about $6.1B, {+ +26% +} on FY25, then $7.1B in FY27E, with EPS rising from $1.52 in FY25 to $1.83 and $2.17.
The latest quarter supports that path: Q2'26 revenue grew much faster than the full-year estimate, so FY26E does not need the quarter's pace to persist.

The counterweight is that the pack does not show how much of the jump is organic. The 10-K states that, as at December 31, 2025, the asset management business's results are consolidated into BAM's financial statements, and the 10-Q's MD&A refers to the completed Oaktree Acquisition. Neither document in the pack quantifies their effect on revenue, so part of the growth may reflect structure rather than new Fee-Bearing Capital.
A dedicated AI infrastructure fund targets demand from hyperscalers, enterprises and governments, extending the infrastructure platform into data and compute buildout.
The private wealth channel, served by semi-liquid products such as an infrastructure income fund, opens a client pool beyond the institutional base.

management.leadership: The pack carries no proxy statement and does not name BAM's executives, so we assess the organization rather than individuals. BAM fields a deep bench of investment and asset management professionals across a wide global office network and draws on Brookfield's heritage as an owner and operator. The 10-Q's MD&A describes integrity as its guiding principle, with a culture of collaboration to attract and retain talent. The MD&A also says the company ensures alignment of interests with clients by investing Brookfield capital alongside them; the pack shows no amount for that investment. We see an organization built for scale, but without named executives we cannot judge the team itself.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation centers on returning cash rather than building assets. Capital expenditure is negligible, and the pack shows no investing or co-investment line, no share repurchases and no total debt. The pack therefore lets us measure no use of cash other than the dividend, whose coverage is the open question set out under cash flow. The payout policy, not reinvestment, is the capital-allocation decision that matters for holders, and it currently relies on sources beyond free cash flow.
management.governance: The pack carries no proxy statement, so board composition and independence, executive pay and related-party terms cannot be assessed from it; we flag that gap rather than infer. Per the company description (September 23, 2026), BAM operates as a subsidiary of Brookfield Corporation. The pack does not show the parent's stake, so the influence it may hold over board and payout decisions cannot be measured here. The 10-K notes that some of BAM's officers and directors are not U.S. residents and that a portion of its assets sits outside the U.S., which may make service of process and enforcement of judgments difficult for investors. We treat the parent relationship as an unquantified risk for outside holders rather than a reason to change the call.
management.insiderOwnership: The pack includes no proxy statement, so insider and significant-shareholder ownership is not disclosed here. The only ownership fact available is the parent-subsidiary relationship noted under governance, and the size of the parent's holding is not in the pack.

idiosyncratic: Distribution coverage: the dividend has run ahead of free cash flow, as detailed under cash flow. If the outside funding that filled the gap becomes less available, the payout or the balance sheet could come under pressure.

Internal-control scope: per the 10-K filed in March 2026, the asset management business's results are consolidated into BAM, but management excluded that business from its evaluation of internal control over financial reporting for FY25 as a result of the 2025 Arrangement, leaving part of reported results outside that assessment.

Non-standard metrics: the 10-K acknowledges that BAM discloses certain metrics without standardized meaning, based on its own methodologies and assumptions, which may complicate comparison across companies and periods.

Street dispersion: the lowest analyst target sits below the current price and the panel is split almost evenly between Buy and Hold, so sentiment could move against the shares if the next quarters disappoint.
risks.systemic: BAM's fee base moves with financial markets and interest rates. The 10-Q's MD&A states that price fluctuations within equity, credit, interest-rate and foreign-exchange markets can be volatile and can have a substantial impact on the business. It also sets the backdrop: U.S. real GDP growth was estimated at 1.7% for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, against 2.1% the prior quarter. The annual U.S. inflation rate rose to 3.5%, and the Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.50%-3.75% in June 2026. Outside the U.S., Eurozone growth stayed subdued, the ECB raised its key rates by 25 basis points, and China's GDP growth slowed to 4.3%. Equity markets rose over the quarter, with the S&P 500 up 14.9% and the MSCI World up 13.3%, which supports asset values, but a reversal would weigh on fundraising and fee-bearing capital. Higher-for-longer rates would also raise the discount applied to the long-duration real assets at the core of BAM's platforms.

body: We rate BAM a BUY with a target range of $50 to $58. Revenue growth has accelerated and free cash flow has improved, and at $46.01 the shares price little of the consensus earnings path. The Base case asks only that consensus EPS arrive and the market hold roughly today's current-year multiple a year out.

Our expected upside is +11.9% with a reward/risk of 0.58x, just over the BUY line; the valuation section sets out why the label is fragile. The payout's reliance on sources beyond free cash flow, the unseparated consolidation effects in revenue and the internal-control exclusion keep conviction moderate. We would move to HOLD if revenue growth falls back below the FY26E consensus pace in the coming quarters, or if cash starts to fall while the payout still exceeds free cash flow.
